elements.quote: Wehave checked the PROSPERO database https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/displayrecord.php?) to see whether recently published or ongoing projects exist related to the topic to avoid any further unnecessary duplication: This systematic review and meta-analysis were registered in the PROSPERO database with ID no. CRD42023442583.
elements.reason: The authors report checking PROSPERO and registering the review to avoid duplication, which addresses consideration of existing similar reviews; however, they do not identify, cite, or discuss any prior similar systematic reviews or explicitly justify the need for this review as an update or replication, so the requirement is only partially met.
This review examines prevalence and predictors of surgical site infection (observational studies), not effects of interventions; no intervention mechanism of action is applicable.
A logic model for complex interventions is not applicable because the review addresses prevalence and predictors rather than evaluating a complex intervention or delivery context.

elements.quote: To determine the pooled prevalence of SSI following cesarean section and its predictors in Ethiopia.
elements.reason: The manuscript gives an explicit, concise statement of the review objective addressing the question the review examines (pooled prevalence and predictors of SSI after cesarean section in Ethiopia).

elements.quote: This SRMA included all articles conducted in all regional state of Ethiopia reporting the prevalence/proportion/incidence of SSI after cesarean section and/or associated factors. All observational study designs (case-control and cross-sectional study designs) were included in this SRMA.
elements.reason: The review examines prevalence and associated factors using observational studies rather than interventions; planned comparisons using PICO for intervention effects do not apply.

elements.quote: This SRMA included all articles conducted in all regional state of Ethiopia reporting the prevalence/proportion/incidence of SSI after cesarean section and/or associated factors. All observational study designs (case-control and cross-sectional study designs) were included in this SRMA.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies setting (regional states of Ethiopia), eligible outcomes (prevalence/incidence of SSI and associated factors) and eligible study designs (case-control, cross-sectional / all observational designs). It does not specify follow-up requirements or other study characteristic details that would fully satisfy the item.

elements.quote: Both published articles and grey literatures published in English language from January 1 2013 to September 2023.
elements.reason: The eligibility criteria explicitly state publication/report status (published and grey literature), language (English), and a date range (Jan 1, 2013 to Sep 2023).

No information is provided that distinguishes excluding studies because outcomes were not measured versus excluding because outcome results were not reported. The only exclusion statement notes studies that 'lack our outcome of interest' without that distinction.

elements.quote: Based on the study region, subgroup analyses were done.
elements.reason: The review specifies at least one grouping used in synthesis (subgroup analyses by study region). However, it does not comprehensively specify all groups used in each synthesis nor explicitly link these groups to the comparisons defined in the review objectives.
Although notable restrictions are applied (e.g., English language, date range), the manuscript does not provide a rationale explaining these restrictions.

elements.quote: The electronic literature search was last performed on September 23, 2023.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the date when the electronic literature search was last performed.

elements.quote: An appropriate and comprehensive search of PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Google Scholar, HINARI and Scopus was done since 2013.
elements.reason: Database names and a general coverage start ('since 2013') are reported, but the search interface/platform for each database and specific coverage date ranges per database are not provided.

elements.quote: This SRMA has comprised of two main outcomes. The primary outcome was magnitude of SSI among women underwent cesarean section, which is defined as the proportion of women after cesarean section who fulfills the CDC criteria of surgical site definition within 30 days of post-partum and it could be at least one of the following: ( A superficial incisional , deep incisional or deep/organ SSI) . The secondary outcome was the determinants of SSI after cesarean section in Ethiopia.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists and defines the two outcome domains (primary: magnitude with CDC definition and subtypes; secondary: determinants).

elements.quote: which is defined as the proportion of women after cesarean section who fulfills the CDC criteria of surgical site definition within 30 days of post-partum

elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the additional variables that were extracted and defined (author, sample size, publication year, study region, study design, prevalence/proportion of SSI, and adjusted ORs with 95% CIs).

elements.quote: A random effect model was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of SSI. Adjusted Odds Ratio (OR) with 95% Confidence Interval (CI) was also considered to determine the association of identified variables with SSI.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly state the effect measures used: pooled prevalence estimated via a random-effects model for the primary outcome (prevalence/proportion) and adjusted odds ratios with 95% CIs for associations (determinants).
No text specifies thresholds or ranges used to interpret effect sizes or provides rationale for such thresholds.
No methods are described for re-expressing synthesized results using another effect measure.

elements.quote: Inclusion. This SRMA included all articles conducted in all regional state of Ethiopia reporting the prevalence/proportion/incidence of SSI after cesarean section and/or associated factors. All observational study designs (case-control and cross-sectional study designs) were included in this SRMA. Both published articles and grey literatures published in English language from January 1 2013 to September 2023. Exclusion. which lack our outcome of interest: SSI following cesarean section and its predictors were excluded from this SRMA. On the other hand, literatures with poor quality as per the criteria of reviewing articles were excluded from this SRMA.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies inclusion and exclusion criteria defining which studies were eligible for the syntheses (studies reporting prevalence/incidence of SSI and/or associated factors; observational designs; date and language limits; exclusion if lacking outcome or poor quality).

elements.quote: The extracted Microsoft Excel spreadsheet format data was imported to STATA software version 17 (STATA corporation, Texas, USA) for analysis. Then random effect model was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of SSI after cesarean section in Ethiopia. Cochrane Q-test and I 2 statistics were computed to assess heterogeneity among all the studies included in this SRMA. Accordingly, if the result of I 2 is 0-40% it is mild heterogeneity, 40 to 70% would be moderate heterogeneity, and 70 to 100% would be considerable heterogeneity [26]. Funnel plot and Eggers test were done to assess publication bias. The p-value > 0.05 indicated that there was no publication bias. Subgroup analysis was done based on the study region. A forest plot format was used to present the pooled prevalence of surgical site infection after cesarean section with 95% CI. To identify determinant factors, we used the pooled AOR in forest plot format with its respective 95%CI.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes some data preparation and presentation steps (exporting data to Excel, importing to STATA, use of random-effects model, heterogeneity metrics, funnel/Egger tests, subgroup and sensitivity analyses, and forest plots). However, it does not explicitly describe methods for handling missing summary statistics or specific data conversions (e.g., how absent variances or differing summary measures were imputed or converted), so the requirement is only partly fulfilled.

elements.quote: Statistical analysis was conducted using STATA version 17 software.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical software and version used for synthesis (STATA version 17).
A meta-analysis was performed, so an alternative synthesis because meta-analysis was impossible does not apply.

elements.quote: A random effect model was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of SSI.
elements.reason: The manuscript states the use of a random-effects model for meta-analysis; additionally, rationale for using random effects to address heterogeneity is provided elsewhere (see chunk text_18).

elements.quote: Then random effect model was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of SSI after cesarean section in Ethiopia. Cochrane Q-test and I 2 statistics were computed to assess heterogeneity among all the studies included in this SRMA.
elements.reason: The statistical method used for pooling (random-effects meta-analysis) and heterogeneity tests (Cochrane Q and I2) are explicitly described.

elements.quote: Cochrane Q-test and I 2 statistics were computed to assess heterogeneity among all the studies included in this SRMA.
elements.reason: Methods to identify and quantify statistical heterogeneity (Cochrane Q and I2) are reported.
The manuscript states a random-effects model was used but does not report the between-study variance estimator (e.g., DerSimonian–Laird, REML).
No information is provided on the method used to calculate confidence intervals for the summary effect in the random-effects meta-analysis.
Other implementation details for the random-effects model (e.g., continuity corrections, weighting scheme) are not reported.
No Bayesian meta-analysis was performed, so prior distributions are not applicable.
The manuscript does not describe methods to account for dependency among multiple estimates from the same study (e.g., multilevel models, robust variance).
The paper does not identify any planned syntheses that were judged impossible or inappropriate nor provide reasons for such decisions.

elements.quote: Based on the study region, subgroup analyses were done. The stability or robustness of the pooled estimates to outliers and the impact of individual studies were assessed using sensitivity analysis.
elements.reason: The methods used to explore heterogeneity are specified: subgroup analysis by study region and sensitivity analysis to assess robustness/outlier impact.

elements.quote: Subgroup analysis was done by using the study region and the result revealed that the pooled prevalence of SSI cesarean section was highest in Amhara region (12.47%; 95% (CI: 7.33, 17.60%), I 2 = 95.28%, P = 0.00) ... observed in Tigray region (8.91%; 95%CI: 4.15, 13.66%), I 2 = 72.24%, P = 0.06) followed by Oromia region (9.18%; 95%CI: 7.16, 11.20%), I 2 = 0.00%, P = 0.77 (Fig 4).
elements.reason: The subgroup factor (study region) and factor levels (Amhara, SNNP, Tigray, Oromia, etc.) and their subgroup estimates are reported, but no expected direction of effect modification is provided.
The report does not state whether subgroup/meta-regression analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both; no explicit information is provided in the retrieved evidence.
Methods used to compare subgroup effects are reported via between-group heterogeneity (Q) tests with corresponding p-values.

elements.quote: Then random effect model was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of SSI after cesarean section in Ethiopia. ... Subgroup analysis was done based on the study region.
elements.reason: Meta-analysis was conducted (random-effects pooled estimates and subgroup analyses used), so the conditional item about informal methods when meta-analysis was unsuitable does not apply.
No information is provided identifying which heterogeneity analyses (e.g. subgroup analyses or sensitivity analyses) were pre-specified versus post-hoc; this is not reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The result of a random effect model revealed that, the pooled prevalence of SSI after cesarean section in Ethiopia was not influenced by a single study (Fig 5).
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that a sensitivity analysis (influence analysis removing single studies) was conducted and gives the result that the pooled prevalence was not influenced by any single study. However, detailed information about every sensitivity analysis performed (methods, exact procedures, or results for all sensitivity checks) is not fully described in the provided evidence, so reporting is partial.

No information is provided in the retrieved evidence indicating which sensitivity analyses were pre-specified or whether any were post-hoc; the manuscript does not identify non–pre-specified sensitivity analyses.

elements.quote: Atotal of 6334 articles were found by using our search strategies: Google scholar, pub-med, Hinari, EMBASE, Scopus and Medline. After 1398 articles were removed for the reason of duplication, 4932 articles left. Then by reviewing their titles and abstracts, 4800 and 100 articles were removed respectively.
elements.reason: The text reports the number of records identified (6334), duplicates removed before screening (1398), the number remaining for screening (4932), and the numbers excluded at title and abstract screening (4800 and 100).

elements.quote: Finally 32 full text papers were accessed and evaluated for the predefined inclusion criteria. Thus 13 more articles were excluded for the afore-mentioned reasons.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the number of reports assessed for eligibility (32) and the number excluded with primary reason (13; outcome not reported per flow chart), but does not explicitly state whether any sought reports were not retrieved (no 'reports sought but not retrieved' number).

elements.quote: Eventually, 19 articles were found eligible for inclusion in the final SRMA (Fig 1).
elements.reason: The text explicitly gives the number of included studies/reports (19) included in the review.

No ongoing studies or associated reports are reported in the manuscript; the authors state they checked PROSPERO for ongoing projects but do not report any ongoing studies relevant to inclusion, so this item is not applicable.
There is no indication that this review is an update of a previous review and no previous-review study counts are reported, so the update-specific reporting requirement does not apply.

The PRISMA flow diagram and text report numbers removed as duplicates and numbers excluded at screening but do not distinguish records excluded by automation versus by humans; no explicit separation is provided.

The provided evidence does not cite the specific studies that appeared to meet inclusion criteria but were excluded, nor does it give per-study reasons for exclusion. elements.quote: Among the studies included in this SRMA, six studies were in Amhara, four in SNNP region, two in Oromia, two in Addis Ababa, two in Harari, one in Dire Dawa and two in Tigray. Fourteen of the studies were cross sectional, four were cohort and one case control studies. A total of 8755 participants with the smallest 166 to the largest 1069 participants included and found the prevalence which ranges from 6.80 to 25.4% of SSI following cesarean section in Ethiopia. On the other hand, the quality of each study was assessed by using NOS, the score of all included studies lies between 8 to 9 which indicates good quality (Table 1) (1).

elements.quote: Atotal of 6334 articles were found by using our search strategies: Google scholar, pub-med, Hinari, EMBASE, Scopus and Medline. After 1398 articles were removed for the reason of duplication, 4932 articles left. Then by reviewing their titles and abstracts, 4800 and 100 articles were removed respectively. Finally 32 full text papers were accessed and evaluated for the predefined inclusion criteria. Thus 13 more articles were excluded for the afore-mentioned reasons. Eventually, 19 articles were found eligible for inclusion in the final SRMA (Fig 1).
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies the set of studies contributing to the synthesis (reports number screened/excluded and states that 19 articles were included); additional tables (e.g. table_3) list contributing study authors, showing which studies contributed to syntheses.

elements.quote: The result of this SRMA showed the overall pooled prevalence of SSI following cesarean section in Ethiopia was 11.13% with a 95% CI: (9.29, 12.97%), which is much higher than the global prevalence of 5.63% [40]. This result is consistent with a study conducted in Rwanda which is 10.9% [14]. However, this was lower than the study conducted in China [15], Jordan [41] and Ekiti state, Nigeria [13] reported 23.3%, 14.4% and 16.01% respectively. ... On the contrary, our study finding was much higher than the studies conducted in developed nations: Ireland [42], Poland [5], Estonia [10] and Egypt [43] reported 0.63%, 0.5%, 6.2% and 5.34% respectively. The inconsistency from these studies might be due to the difference in health care facility, thus evidence based practice and effective infection prevention mechanisms are more likely to be practiced in developed countries. ... This review has also identified the factors associated with SSI following cesarean section in Ethiopia. Prolonged labor, chorioamnionitis, prolonged PROM, vertical skin incision, decreased post- operative HGB, repeated vaginal examination and general anesthesia were found to be the independent risk factors of surgical site infection following cesarean section in Ethiopia. Women who had prolonged labor were 3.16 times more likely to develop SSI than their counterparts. The finding was similar with the studies conducted in Cross river state, Nigeria [44] and Egypt [43].
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly compares the pooled prevalence and identified predictors to results from other studies (global estimates and studies from Rwanda, China, Jordan, Nigeria, Ireland, Poland, Estonia, Egypt, etc.), explains similarities and differences, and offers possible reasons for discrepancies, fulfilling interpretation in the context of other evidence.
